report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is **true**, not false, for reduction of *breast-cancer incidence* in the studied population—postmenopausal women at increased risk. It does **not** establish reduced breast-cancer mortality or prove a favorable net benefit for every individual.

The central evidence is MAP.3, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 4,560 such women. At median follow-up of about 3 years, invasive breast cancer occurred substantially less often with exemestane: reported relative reduction 65% (hazard ratio 0.35). This is strong causal evidence for lower short-term incidence, although the absolute number of cancers was small and follow-up was relatively short. The trial found more overall adverse events with exemestane (88% vs 85%), but no statistically significant difference in fractures, cardiovascular events, other cancers, or treatment-related deaths during that follow-up. https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1103507

Reasons one might resist an overbroad version of the claim: benefit is principally expected for estrogen-receptor–positive cancers; evidence for long-term harms and outcomes such as mortality is limited; and aromatase inhibitors can cause vasomotor, gastrointestinal, and musculoskeletal symptoms. The USPSTF consequently frames these drugs as options for women at increased risk who are also at low risk for medication harms—not as universal prevention. https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/document/evidence-summary/breast-cancer-medications-for-risk-reduction

Thus, the evidence supports “reduces incidence” but not “prevents all breast cancer,” “reduces deaths,” or “is appropriate for all elevated-risk women.”
